## Amy Sartran ([@asartran](https://github.com/asartran))

### What you did this week

- Got the Snowball training loop ready, 2 nodes of MI355x. Checkpointing, restarts and real data all work. Built the Snowball-mix ladder datasets on GCS, and drafted an outline for a decontaminated Harrier training set for the full snowball run.
- Mostly reviewing and benchmarking Marco’s AMD PR stack(#11122-#11126, #11140-#11148, #11150-#11159). We’re reworking to avoid touching too much of the model config and having AMD-specific implementation logic outside the training code.
- Some CI fixes. One makes pre-commit catch stale vendored lockfiles, which failed 87 CI jobs last week ([#11423](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11423)). The other fixes one of the two failures that have broken the nightly slow job since Nov 3 [#11425](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11425), [#11427](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11427).

sourceStates.body:
Grade RLVR-IFeval descriptors, skyrl-gym IFEval rollouts and preflight, and Evalchemy harness IFEval through verifyit. Remove both open-instruct checker copies and the unused harness copy. IFBench keeps its separate source checkers.

Score changes affect `MarinSkyRL:rlvr_ifeval`, skyrl-gym `ifeval`, and `Evalchemy:ifeval`. The previously unpatched skyrl-gym path now accepts the four reported formatting cases; verifyit's language, punctuation, sentence, and Markdown checks also differ from the source checkers. The RLVR curation source advances from version 1 to 2. Evalchemy IFEval advances from protocol 2026.11.02 to 2026.11.22 and receives a new content-derived scorer revision. The frozen Micro210 policy and prepared task bytes remain unchanged.

Regression coverage exercises the four reported cases through the migrated paths, including replies that ignore each instruction. Focused tests and Pyrefly pass. The affected-test runner passed 2,049 Harbor tests, then stopped before root pytest because its local environment lacks `pytest-xdist`.

Fixes #11984

sourceStates.title: [ifeval] Correct repeat and language grading
sourceStates.body:
Harness IFEval now compares `combination:repeat_prompt` with the source `prompt_to_repeat` after trimming and lowercasing, so a reply can repeat only the request before answering. Harness language constraints use `langdetect==1.0.9` seeded to zero. The detector returns `en` for all three reported English counterexamples and `de` for a German control sentence. Detection errors fail the constraint; a missing detector package surfaces as a grader infrastructure error.

RLVR-IFeval curation and skyrl-gym preflight reject response-language descriptors because their grader retains the hint-word check. The IFEval protocol advances to `2026.11.22.1` and the RLVR source advances to version 3 so changed scores have distinct identities.

sourceStates.title: [levanter] Use exact replay scoring in the policy learner
sourceStates.body:
Use the same fixed FP32 vocabulary projection and normalization in native Snowball serving and the policy learner when `with_zero_kl_replay()` is selected. The binary adapter requires one right-padded trajectory per row and rejects unsupported layouts before attaching the served routes and scores.

On one v4-8 host, the four-slot TPU fixture carried 32 sampled token scores into the clipped policy objective. All 32 served raw policy log probabilities matched the learner's recomputed values bit for bit. The maximum absolute old/current log-ratio was zero, and the KL term was zero with a positive coefficient and the serving snapshot as the reference. [TPUv4 run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fsnowball-upstream-unified-learner-zero-kl-frame-v4-20261123)

Depends on #12067 and #12070.

sourceStates.title: [rl] Select the native Snowball learner in SkyRL
sourceStates.body:
Select the isolated Snowball policy learner with `trainer.strategy: levanter`. SkyRL reserves one whole GPU bundle per learner node. Each bundle runs one JAX child process, and the configured model mesh spans those processes. The host sends complete optimizer minibatches after SkyRL has calculated their advantages.

This strategy requires separate policy and rollout nodes and the KL penalty disabled. The JAX learner stages frozen weights in host memory, and the existing Torch expert-block sender publishes those slices to compiled vLLM over NCCL. Native checkpoints preserve learner state across restarts. #12073 separately verifies bitwise serving and learner log probabilities on TPUv4 with a positive KL coefficient.

All 74 Marin launch tests and 16 SkyRL config and batch tests passed on CPU. A composed accelerator launch is pending.

Depends on #12077.

sourceStates.body:
Add a proof of concept that finds eval items in pretraining records in two stages, with one rule for every required eval (1,554,277 records) and no values set per eval. The code, commands, results and limits are in `experiments/datakit/decontam/encoder`.

Stage 1 keys each item by the rarest 20-character window of its text stream (lowercase letters and digits). The rarity comes from 264 reference shards, and a record that holds an item's key becomes a candidate. Records are also read with their JSON escapes undone once and twice: in the plain stream, `\n` before a word reads as a LaTeX command and removes the word, so an item stored in a JSON dump keeps only about two thirds of its windows. Stage 2 fine-tunes `jhu-clsp/mmBERT-base` on (item, record excerpt) pairs. `left` holds the question, its choices and its answer, and a hint lists the question words and the answer words that the excerpt lacks. The model gives two probabilities: the record holds the question, and the record holds the question with its answer.

Weighted by source size, key 1 marks 0.09-0.10% of records, both on the calibration shards and on 128 new validation shards. That is 4.2e7 candidates for the catalog, about 27 H100-hours of scoring, and stage 1 itself takes about 24,000 CPU worker-hours. The JSON readings leave the load unchanged, raise key recall on judged copies from 0.882 to 0.932, and cost 38% more stage-1 CPU.

Training uses synthetic copies and variants written into real record text, 20,000 silver negatives, and three label sets of real stage-1 candidates (1,757 pairs on which both judges agree, 326 of them copies). Codex and Claude label the candidates blind with `RUBRIC.md`. On the key-1 test pairs (260 pairs, 118 copies), the reference model gives:

| Score at least | Marks | Precision [5% bound] | Recall |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | 105 | 0.87 [0.80] | 0.77 |
| 0.99 | 70 | 0.94 [0.88] | 0.56 |

On 128 new validation shards, with keys, models and thresholds frozen before labeling (338 agreed pairs, 160 copies), precision weighted to the candidate pool at score 0.99 is 0.971 (bootstrap 5% bound 0.941) for the reference model and 0.980 (0.954) for the iteration-10 model, at 62-64% recall of the high-overlap copies. 106 of the 160 copies are DROP short questions; without DROP, 16-21 marks are too few for a bound.

Planted copies of 41,350 items from all 827 evals, in 14 forms, test stage 1. It finds every copy in the plain, label-style, no-line-break, extra-option and JSON-escaped forms. It misses short items in layouts without choice letters (2.9% of all items, mostly ZhoBLiMP and BBQ, whose key holds the letters), some LaTeX copies without backslashes, and casing that does not round-trip.

The precision target, a lower bound of at least 0.95 on real candidates, is met on validation only by the iteration-10 model, and only over all evals. With precision near 0.95, a bound of 0.95 needs several hundred labeled marks. One training run is also noisy: the same recipe gave set-11 test AUCs of 0.973 and 0.948, so recipes were compared with two seeds on the pooled test. The choice input and the answer-free question hint raised question AUC from 0.950 / 0.960 to 0.971 / 0.968. Labeling the answer only in layouts that mark it raised answer AUC from 0.922 to 0.958 / 0.943.

The item table reads choices from option fields, parsed prompts and lettered choices. It also reads DROP answers: the lm-eval target template joins the answer object, so it had rendered the answer's key names.

sourceStates.title: [rl] Stop code and Reasoning Gym replies from setting their own reward
sourceStates.body:
The vendored LiveCodeBench evaluator now compares outputs outside the process that runs the program, and the Reasoning Gym scorers that evaluate text receive a reply only when evaluating it cannot run code. Before, a reply could score 1.0 on the code and Reasoning Gym tasks of `snowball-100k` without solving them (the issue, #11990).

The evaluator (`datasets/skyrl/scorers/livecodebench.py`, also shipped to the Ultra competitive-coding tasks) ran and judged each test in one child process: `grade_stdio` held the expected output in `gt_out` while the program ran, `grade_call_based` decided with `prediction == gt_out`, and the child pickled its own verdict to the parent. A program could print `gt_out` from the evaluator's frame, return an object whose `__eq__` returns `True`, or send a passing verdict over the child's pipe. The child now receives the program and the test inputs, runs each input under the same per-test alarm and `reliability_guard`, and sends what the program returned or printed as JSON. The parent compares with the expected output, keeps the first-failure exit and every metadata field, and stops the child once it has a verdict. Return values cross with type tags and are rebuilt as the same type (builtins, numpy scalars, `Fraction`, `Decimal`, `complex`), so `==` and the tuple-to-list step give the old results; a builtin subclass becomes its base type, and any other type fails as a wrong answer. The child is spawned rather than forked: a forked child inherits the parent's memory, and with `fork` a program that searches the stack for the test cases still passes.

Nine reasoning-gym 0.1.25 scorers pass the reply to `eval` (`n_queens`, `binary_matrix`, `spiral_matrix`, `string_insertion`) or `sympy.parse_expr` (`polynomial_multiplication`, `simple_integration`, `intermediate_integration`, `puzzle24`, `countdown`); an audit hook on `compile` over all 104 generated tasks finds no other. `_score_candidate`, which all three grading paths call, now passes a reply to them only when it is in the answer's own form or a Python literal (the `eval` tasks), or an arithmetic expression over numbers, SymPy math and names that `parse_expr` turns into new symbols (the `parse_expr` tasks). Any other reply is scored as the empty reply: 0.0, or the 0.01 that `countdown` and `puzzle24` give any reply they cannot parse.

On main `f8e4c0a43`:

| reply | main | this change |
|---|---:|---:|
| stdin program printing `gt_out` from the evaluator's frame, 113 sampled stdin rows | 113 | 1 |
| stdin program sending a passing verdict over the pipe, same rows | 113 | 0 |
| call-based return equal to everything, 6 sampled rows | 6 | 0 |
| Reasoning Gym reply registering an `atexit` handler that prints `1.0`, both grade scripts, 109 rows | 109 | 0 |
| Reasoning Gym reply returning the stored answer from `/tests/config.json`, 53 `parse_expr` rows | 41 | 0 |

The one stdin row still paid expects empty output for its only test, so printing nothing is right there.

Verdicts of honest programs do not change. The code rows are seeded samples of `eurus2_code` and Ultra `comp_coding` (119 converted rows). On them, 865 grades of table-lookup programs (correct, last test wrong, first number off by one), constants, echoes, crashes, early exits, infinite loops, hand-written solutions of 15 rows and call-based returns as tuples give the same reward, per-test results and metadata on both trees. 94 call-based returns of eight JSON types and their variants (numpy scalars, `Fraction`, `Decimal`, subclasses, sets, generators) give the same rewards; the one metadata difference is a returned numpy array, a wrong answer on both trees, now reported as a wrong answer instead of an ambiguous-truth runtime error. On the 9,000 generated entries and 175 Ultra rows of the nine Reasoning Gym tasks, each entry's own answer scores 1.0 on both trees and 66,183 other non-code replies (wrong answers, list literals, reordered terms, an integration constant named `K`) score the same.

Each graded code reply now starts a Python interpreter for the child, which imports numpy and pandas: on the code sample, 1,196 grades took 394.6 s instead of 40.5 s, 0.30 s more per reply. A script that calls the evaluator must guard its entry point, as `spawn` requires; both grade scripts do.

A program can still open `/tests/config.json`, the grade script's own input, which holds the test cases; through the grade scripts it scores 1.0 on 18 of 18 rows on both trees. Closing that needs the grading machine to keep the cases out of the program's reach and is not part of this change.

Part of #11990.

sourceStates.title: [eval] Shuffle TruthfulQA choices in a new Micro210 policy
sourceStates.body:
Build a new Micro210 policy that permutes each TruthfulQA task's choices with a seed derived from its stable task ID. The prompt, accepted verifier letters, likelihood requests, and target index move together. Each task records its seed and source-index permutation. The build rejects any lettered-choice benchmark with a universally accepted letter.

The pinned 440-row prepared table keeps task selection and every non-TruthfulQA row unchanged. With the frozen grader, constant `A` scores 10/10 on the old TruthfulQA rows and 3/10 on the new rows; the best constant letter scores 5/10. GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro have no universal correct letter, so their scores do not change. Model TruthfulQA scores require a new run. The [new policy](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#gs%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east1%2Fevaluation-policies%2Fmicro210%2F2026.11.23-choice-shuffle%2Fd99573b7d8e8801014e01afdcec0d53b7f3e857cf487556045be137392f28e59%2Fpolicy.json) is staged at `gs://marin-us-east1/evaluation-policies/micro210/2026.11.23-choice-shuffle/d99573b7d8e8801014e01afdcec0d53b7f3e857cf487556045be137392f28e59/policy.json` (SHA-256 `d99573b7d8e8801014e01afdcec0d53b7f3e857cf487556045be137392f28e59`); the table SHA-256 is `0cf6f6de9f9b68273b4954e25710cf83a3df522d01883af2e07ed0f03cdc44f3`.

The policy and private prepared table still need immutable Hugging Face commits before the launcher can select this version. The publication script checks readback and private access. Until those commits are available, the launcher keeps its existing policy pin. Unit tests and a local full-table rebuild pass; no model score has been rerun under the new version.

diagnostics.body:
Snapshot of realized step times, token volumes and GPU allocations for Mochi and Snowball RL and SFT, taken on 2026-11-23 from Finelog trainer markers, run logs and #8089. ## SFT

| Model / run | GPUs | Tokens per step | Realized step | Throughput |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mochi SFT production run (#8089, 10.05 mix) | 11 GB200 NVL72 racks (~792 GPUs) | 176 × 262,144 ≈ 46.1M | 29.3 s median; 6,916 updates in 58.0 h | ~1.57M tok/s, ~2.0k tok/s/GPU |
| Mochi SFT run on cw-us-east-08a, 2026-11-23 | 128 GB200 | 32 × 262,144 ≈ 8.4M (from logged hyperparameters) | 9.3 s/it | ~0.90M tok/s, ~7.0k tok/s/GPU |
| Snowball Exp5 SFT (V7 mix) | 256 H100 | ≈ 67M, assuming 256 × 262,144 packing as in V9 (not read from this run's logs) | ~115 s/it trainer rate; ~124 s wall (475 steps in 16 h 25 min) | ~0.58M tok/s, ~2.3k tok/s/GPU |

## Observations

- RL realized time is about 10× the training step for both models. Evaluation and rollout-buffer refill dominate, not optimizer compute.
- Per step, Snowball Exp5 consumes about 4× Mochi's response tokens (512 vs 256 sequences, longer agentic histories) in similar realized time.
- Mochi SFT on 128 GB200 delivers about 3.5× the per-GPU token throughput of the 11-rack run.

diagnostics.title: [long-loop] Ablate the RL learning rate for Mochi and Snowball on the best curriculum
diagnostics.body:
Mochi and Snowball long-loop RL used learning rates an order of magnitude apart: Mochi `.123` ran at 1e-5 and Snowball Exp5 `.140` at 1e-6. Neither value came from an ablation. From Exp6 (Snowball) and the next Mochi round, both models use the Snowball defaults: 1e-6, `max_grad_norm` 0.5 and 64 prompts × 8 samples per batch. This experiment should settle whether that learning rate is right for each model. It is planned here and not yet scheduled.

Design:
- Curriculum: our best RL curriculum at the time it runs, identical for both models. Record its identity and version.
- Fixed settings: the normalized config for all other settings (staleness 3, 98,304-token response cap and 131,072-token context, batch 64 × 8, `max_grad_norm` 0.5), one seed per arm, and the frozen 200-row validation split from the curriculum.
- Grid: half-decade steps, starting at 3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6 and 1e-5 for each model.
- Metric: an EMA of validation accuracy over the first 20 optimizer updates (EMA window 5, matching best-checkpoint selection). Report raw per-eval accuracy and training reward alongside it.
- Adaptive grid: if the best arm is at either edge of the grid, add the next half-decade step beyond that edge and repeat until the best value is interior.
- Stability checks per arm: training/inference mismatch KL, gradient norm and the clipped-gradient fraction. Report any divergence as a result, not a rerun.

Done when:
- Both models have a learning-rate curve whose best value is interior to the grid, with EMA validation accuracy at 20 updates per arm.
- A recommended learning rate per model is stated, with the stability metrics that support it.
- The long-loop RL defaults are updated, or confirmed unchanged, from that recommendation.

diagnostics.title: [rl] Track the Snowball RL resizing sprint (65k decode, right-sized layout)
diagnostics.body:
## TL;DR

A ~12-hour PRODUCTION-priority sprint (opened 2026-11-21 ~23:00 EST per the user request) to (1) maximize Snowball decode throughput at the 65,536-token request window and (2) size the Snowball RL job as small as possible while keeping training saturated (rollout wait near zero, no time-per-update regression vs the current baseline). Deliverable: a right-sized Snowball RL layout (GPU counts, engine config, all gates) with its measured time per update vs the current allocation and the GPU-hours cost per update. This issue is maintained by the secretary agent from the worker's REPORT.md/STATUS.md; every measured arm is recorded as it lands with reproduction details.

## Description

Context: Snowball RL runs on the Exp4/Exp5 long-loop pools (H100 on cw-rno2a; Snowball also ran on cw-us-east-08a GB200 for the Nov 20 acceptance, job `.305`, 40 GB200). The playbook and lessons come from the Mochi sprint (#11954, closed) and its concurrency-gate table (#11957).

Two phases:
- **Phase 1 — decode throughput at 65k context**: pure serving-benchmark arms with the exact Snowball RL rollout engine config, measured with native vLLM counters (aggregate and per-GPU generated tok/s, per-request tok/s, running/waiting per engine, KV use, prefix-hit rate, preemptions, TTFT) on a long-prompt 65,536-token workload with group-shared prompts as in RL.
- **Phase 2 — right-size the RL job**: shrink rollout GPUs and trainer GPUs step by step on real rollouts with the current Snowball curriculum (Exp4/Exp5 pools); report time per update, rollout wait, engine occupancy, and the per-step split (rollout wait / optimizer / checkpoint / eval). Saturated = trainer rollout wait per step near zero and time per update not regressing vs baseline.

Fixed infrastructure/rules for all arms: PRODUCTION priority; GPU budget ≤ ~2 racks / 128 GPUs in flight without coordinator approval; do not disturb Exp5 SFT (256 H100 on cw-rno2a); one knob per arm, config over code; each arm cancelled with `iris-cancel-own` once measured (25-min windows); Harbor ≤ 512 (Daytona RL org shared, one job ~1/4–1/3 of its 6,000 vCPU); long jobs' IDs go to the coordinator watchdog, no polling loops.

diagnostics.title: SWE-bench-style graders record reward 0.0 for fully passing test suites (the F2P/P2P parse fails to match the suite output)
diagnostics.body:
### Summary
The SWE-bench-style shared graders (the taskcompendium log parsers behind the SWE_REBENCH profile) record reward 0.0 for rows whose full test suites PASS in an identical environment. The F2P/P2P parse fails to match the config's test ids against the suite output, so fully-passing suites score 0.0.

### Evidence (SWE-rebench V2.1 repaired wave, the sealed canonical)
The wave's oracle verdicts for three rows, compared against diagnostic runs of the SAME setup + gold patch + test command in the same environment family (the full captures linked below):

| instance | wave oracle reward | diagnostic run |
|---|---|---|
| blitz-js__superjson-78 | 0.0 | Test Suites: 8 passed, 8 total; Tests: 48 passed, 48 total |
| goplus__gop-1659 | 0.0 | 26 `ok` package markers, 0 `FAIL` |
| segmentio__encoding-45 | 0.0 | `--- PASS`, `PASS`, `ok` — 0 `FAIL` |

The suites are fully green; the recorded oracle rewards are 0.0.

### Suspected mechanism
The family config's test ids (FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS) are matched against the suite output by the taskcompendium log parser (parse_log_node for jest, the go-test parser for go). The parsed test names do not match the ids' form (the describe-block-qualified jest names vs the ids' form; the go package-level output), so the parse reports 0 matches and the reward collapses to 0.0.

diagnostics.title: [levanter] Final hook skew aborts multi-host SFT during JAX shutdown
diagnostics.body:
Slow final hooks can turn completed optimizer updates and a saved final checkpoint into a failed multi-host job.

Reproduce:
1. Initialize two JAX processes with `shutdown_timeout_seconds=2`.
2. Delay process 0 for 5 seconds after computation, while process 1 calls `jax.distributed.shutdown()`.
3. Both processes abort. The shutdown barrier reports 1/2 processes present and process 0 missing. This CPU reproduction was run locally; it does not exercise GPU kernels or object-store uploads.

Observed on a 32-process H100 SFT run at source `cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65` on 2026-11-22:
- Process 0 completed step 527 (528 updates) at 16:14:10UTC. Its native checkpoint committed at 16:15:27UTC; the HF export finished at 16:35UTC.
- Processes 1–31 logged completion of their final XLA-dump uploads at 16:39:33–43UTC. Process 0 has no corresponding upload-completion line.
- At16:41:33UTC, the shutdown barrier failed with 31/32 processes present. Process 27 entered first; process 0 was missing.
- Process 1's Python stack ends in `jax.distributed.shutdown()`, called by `_finalize_iris_jax_after_clean_exit`. Iris reports exit 139. The PyArrow/Torch names are the loaded-extension footer, not a causal stack.
- The task timeout was 72000 seconds. The failure occurred at the 120-second JAX shutdown deadline after the first process entered shutdown.
- The training completion receipt was not published. The exact operation delaying process 0 is not recoverable from the fatal signal-handler dump; final-hook/upload skew is supported by the logs, but an upload deadlock is not proven.

The relevant paths are [the Levanter exit handler](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/levanter/src/levanter/distributed.py#L36), [the forced final hooks](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L738), [the synchronous dump uploader](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/levanter/src/levanter/callbacks/profiler.py#L190), and [Iris's shutdown timeout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/cf9db0ac38e2f64eaa917979bbcc4efa98158b65/lib/iris/src/iris/jax/init.py#L48).

Expected: all processes finish required finalization before distributed shutdown starts. Publish the committed-checkpoint/control receipt before optional debug uploads. Bound those uploads and use a symmetric, bounded finalization rendezvous before shutdown. A delayed-process regression must preserve genuine training failures and must not relabel an unfinished checkpoint as complete.

Related closed incidents: #6907 and #7372 involved W&B teardown. This occurrence shows final-hook skew before the completion receipt; the process 0 blocker remains to be isolated.

additionalTopicChecks.title: [rl] Enable frozen DSpark for Snowball RL
additionalTopicChecks.body:
Default to four proposals from the frozen Dr. Doom DSpark draft for Snowball presets that use the pinned Grug-67B-A2B Datakit SFT 09.21 initializer. The draft shares the existing vLLM GPUs. `speed-short` uses a 0.80 GPU memory fraction for its generation burst. The other presets use 0.75. Presets that accept settings support `generator.speculative_decoding=null` for plain decoding. An alternate initializer can supply its own compatible draft. [Pinned draft checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/atutej/dspark_grug-67b-a2b-datakit-sft-dr-doom_datakit-sft-mix_targetgen-warm80k-20261020/tree/d22f4f21ce5cc0968dfd8e2c0d06aaf4adacbbf2) ```mermaid flowchart LR Inputs["09.21 initializer
Pinned Snowball tasks
Frozen DSpark"] --> Short["speed-short vLLM
8 H100s · 4 proposals · 0.80 memory"] Inputs --> Medium["speed-medium vLLM
8 H100s · 4 proposals · 0.75 memory"] Short --> Generation["512 prompts × 4 replies"] Short --> Eval["Separate held-out EvalLite pass"] Medium --> Score["Score rollouts"] Score --> Learner["10 policy updates
32 learner H100s"] Learner -->|"Sync policy weights"| Medium ``` ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant D as Frozen DSpark participant P as Current policy in vLLM loop Each draft round P->>D: Context and policy hidden states D->>P: Sampled proposals and probabilities P->>P: Score proposals and apply rejection sampling Note right of P: Emit accepted prefix and a correction or bonus token end ``` SkyRL’s Nov 18 vLLM wheel supports dense drafts with an expert-parallel target. The checkpoint uses Qwen3-style draft layers. vLLM #128 adds a separate Grug-layer drafter. [Wheel release](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261118-47a8e415bff1) · [Expert-parallel support](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/118) · [Grug-layer drafter](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/128) ### Proposal count at training load The three `speed-medium` attempts used the same wheel, pinned `snowball-100k@2026.11.19.1` data, 0.75 vLLM memory, eight inference H100s and 32 learner H100s. Each consumed 20.97M response tokens over ten updates. The update window starts after the first weight sync and ends after the tenth. | Setting | Median update, 2–10 | Elapsed updates 2–10 | Successful rollout-group p95 | Fresh-policy KL | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Plain | 85.32s | 742s | 88.4s | 0.001179 | | DSpark, 8 proposals | 68.67s | 619s | 94.8s | 0.001239 | | DSpark, 4 proposals | 56.46s | 467s | 64.7s | 0.001273 | Four proposals reduced median update time by 17.8% and elapsed updates 2–10 by 24.6% versus eight. Against fresh plain, four proposals reduced median update time by 33.8% and elapsed updates 2–10 by 37.1%. Both proposal counts passed the calibrated speed and KL guards against four pinned plain controls. [Four-proposal gate](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fpower%2Fcheckpoints%2Fsnowball-rl%2Fspeed-medium-da9cc74fcc-in-9bb30c01%2Fgate-n1-e067447cc5-defaults-19d432b0-evidence-21f4a03c%2F2026.11.13%2Fgate_report.md) · [Eight-proposal gate](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fpower%2Fcheckpoints%2Fsnowball-rl%2Fspeed-medium-da9cc74fcc-in-d38885bb%2Fgate-n1-e067447cc5-defaults-19d432b0-evidence-f866080f%2F2026.11.13%2Fgate_report.md) · [Plain gate](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fpower%2Fcheckpoints%2Fsnowball-rl%2Fspeed-medium-da9cc74fcc-in-8037ac9b%2Fgate-n1-e067447cc5-defaults-19d432b0-evidence-8d5efd55%2F2026.11.13%2Fgate_report.md) | Full-attempt phase | Plain | 8 proposals | 4 proposals | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Attempt start to first rollout | 563s | 537s | 547s | | Update 1 | 141s | 237s | 133s | | Updates 2–10 | 742s | 619s | 467s | | Final sync to terminal receipt | 51s | 64s | 65s | | Native wall | 24m57s | 24m17s | 20m12s | Native wall measures the successful attempt. Four proposals cut native wall by 19.0% versus fresh plain and 16.8% versus eight. The three attempts used 16.63, 16.19, and 13.47 H100-hours, respectively. In the previous calibration the 33s average startup gap came mostly from preparing the 100,000-task dataset before vLLM startup. Engine initialization itself differed by 4s on average. ### Cache and short generation Peak sampled KV occupancy in the training runs was 34.2% plain, 39.6% with eight, and 38.6% with four. The engine requeues in-flight requests when a weight sync invalidates their old KV blocks. The preemption count includes those requeues, so raising the training cache budget has little support from the sampled occupancy. With four proposals the draft emitted 2.53 tokens per verification round in both updates 2–4 and updates 8–10. Eight proposals emitted 3.04 across the measured window. The draft stays frozen. [Pinned vLLM KV reset](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/47a8e415bff1/vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py#L2699-L2727) In the eight-H100 `speed-short` screen, four proposals at 0.80 reached 5,733 tokens/s/GPU versus 5,820 plain (−1.5%, within the 2.37% tolerance). EvalLite was 0.5279 versus 0.5268 across 1,500 held-out tasks. Eight proposals at 0.80 reached 5,472 tokens/s/GPU and failed the throughput guard. The complete four-proposal screen took 11m42s versus 12m45s for the plain mean, including startup and EvalLite. [Four-proposal short gate](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fusers%2Fpower%2Fcheckpoints%2Fsnowball-rl%2Fcompare%2Fspeed-short-9ffe8134%2Fgate-n1-ceae991ad0-defaults-3172f522-evidence-e37562f2%2F2026.11.13%2Fgate_report.md) At update 10 the policy losses were 4.52×10⁻⁶ plain, −1.94×10⁻⁶ with eight, and 1.85×10⁻⁵ with four. Training pass@4 was 14.06%, 17.19%, and 16.41%, respectively. A held-out checkpoint comparison measures learning quality. The four-proposal run had 96.7% stale loss-bearing tokens, compared with 41.7% in the matched plain run. A prior plain control reached 99.4%, so the async scheduler can produce the high-staleness regime in either mode. The benchmark covers the standard 40-H100 training layout. Target-specific offline training for Snowball or Mochi is tracked separately. [Offline trainer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12000) The control-derived tolerances and run invariants follow the Snowball default-change workflow. Refresh production controls and run leave-one-out comparisons after merge. [Benchmark gates](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/recipes/rl-experiments.md#compare-with-controls) · [Default-change workflow](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/recipes/rl-experiments.md#change-a-presets-default)

additionalTopicChecks.title: [grug] Add a one-array RMS rule for MoE expert banks in moe_hero_ep
additionalTopicChecks.body:
Add a `bank_optimizer` enum (`muonh`, `adam`, `rms`) on `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep` to select the update rule for the three 4-D MoE expert-bank arrays (`w_gate`, `w_up`, `w_down`). The default remains `muonh`, leaving existing runs unchanged (`23 muonh / 1 adamh / 12 adam` across the 36 parameter arrays). Selecting `rms` routes the three expert banks to an RMSProp-style second-moment-only rule with no momentum (`optax.scale_by_rms` with `beta2`, `epsilon`, `eps_in_sqrt=False`, and `bias_correction=True`, scaled by `-adam_lr` and omitting `gate_router_weight_decay`), giving `20 muonh / 1 adamh / 12 adam / 3 adam_rms` with one FP32 `nu` array per bank plus a group step counter.

When resuming a `bank_optimizer=rms` run from a checkpoint whose expert banks were saved under `muonh`, the restore path inspects the checkpoint manifest, masks only the four moved `adam_rms` leaves (the three `nu` arrays and the `adam_rms` count) while keeping `allow_partial=False`, and zero-initializes those four leaves directly in their abstract template sharding. The other 33 optimizer slots continue from the checkpoint, and missing non-bank leaves still fail with `FileNotFoundError`. Restore migration applies only to `rms`; restoring `adam` from a `muonh` checkpoint still fails closed.

Extend `log_device_memory` to log HBM peak, live, and limit GiB for every local device (raising if `memory_stats()` returns `None`) and `/proc/self/status` `VmPin`, `VmRSS`, and `VmHWM` in GiB (propagating `OSError`).

At Mochi's `(48, 384, 3072, 3072)` FP32 expert-bank shape, three `nu` arrays total 2.09 TB (1.898 TiB, or 30.38 GiB per GPU across 64 GPUs), matching the persistent state size of Muon-H's `momentum_buffer`. On 64 GPUs at Mochi's real shapes, peak HBM per GPU was 130.288 GiB with this rule and fresh bank state, and 131.688 GiB with 20 gradient-only warm-up passes added in a later change, against 131.430 GiB for the Muon-H control, out of a 143.754 GiB limit.

The Mochi probes of this rule did not pass the written rule (mean loss within 1.05x of the Muon-H twin and no grad norm above 5): the best, with a warm second moment and a 0.25x bank learning rate, reached 1.079x the twin with grad norms up to 10.44. The results and the decision to stop the Mochi Bank-RMS line are in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7080948760.

Part of #11858.

additionalTopicChecks.title: MuonH implementation includes the Expert dimension in the frobenius norm computation for 4D inputs
additionalTopicChecks.body:
As of #7820 the expert FF parameters are stored in a big `[n_layers, n_experts, d_in, d_out]` tensor, eg `[48, 384, 3072, 3072]`, with the specialised [`_newtonschulz_4d_distributed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L211) computing Newton Schulz on the last two dimensions.

However, in the optimizer, the axes used to compute the norm will end up as `(1,2,3)`, which includes the expert dimension.

https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5da0277745729230801f91e0181406f291099f9d/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py#L76

This seems to be unintentional, since that optimizer code was originally to handle 3D `[n_experts, d_in, d_out]` shapes in #6153.

The implication is that an updated matrix parameter **M**<sub>t+1</sub> will **no longer be constrained to its original hypersphere** of norm ||**M**<sub>t</sub>||<sub>F</sub> as described in MuonH originally. Instead the combined cat([**M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t+1</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...]) will be constrained to norm ||cat([**M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert1</sup>, **M**<sub>t</sub><sup>expert2</sup>, ...])||<sub>F</sub> allowing individual matrices to grow or shrink within that constraint. Although not necessarily a terrible thing to do (experiments in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5253 tried both for AdamH).

additionalTopicChecks.title: [eval] Evaluate Hero at multiple context lengths
additionalTopicChecks.body:
Hero evals score 4K and the current training length, adding fixed 65K and 262K evals only once training reaches those lengths. Each distinct length has its own metrics, such as `eval_dropless/seq_len_4096/paloma/macro_loss`; `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` continues to report the training-length eval.

All eval lengths keep the training context-parallel width. The dropless mesh and PartitionSpec renaming reuse #10709's implementation: each device retains its training context group and uses its training (data, expert) group for eval data. Eval therefore reuses the device groups whose replacement caused NCCL memory growth in #10709. Batch sizes stay within the configured global padded-token budget per evaluation batch, rounded down to whole batch shards.

Continuous-text validation retains incomplete final sequences with right padding and excludes padding from attention and loss, including the real-to-pad prediction. Short Paloma corpora remain in the long-context aggregate. Validation sequence statistics include the final partial sequence; stored token counts exclude padding. Overall loss and bits-per-byte macros exclude tags with no scored tokens.

CPU tests check device groups, per-device parameter shards and the multi-length eval-to-training handoff. No GPU rehearsal of this revision has run.
